Densiﬁcation Converses for Walker Constellations
With Explicit Constants and Reuse Scaling Laws
Ali Khalesi and François Baccelli
Abstract—We establish densiﬁcation converses for Walker
LEO constellations under nearest-visible association in the full-
frequency-reuse setting. Performance is evaluated under the
invariant (stationary) measure induced by the constellation/Earth
dynamics on the user–constellation “phase state.” A key Walker-
speciﬁc feature, absent from unbounded planar models, is that
association is restricted to a bounded visible cap determined by
Earth geometry. Under power-law path-loss, a two-level antenna-
gain model, i.i.d. nonnegative fading with unit mean and ﬁnite
second moment, and nonzero noise, we prove that increasing the
total satellite count N = NoNs forces the aggregate interference
to grow at least linearly in N, while the useful signal remains
uniformly bounded above. Consequently, the downlink SINR cov-
erage probability at any ﬁxed threshold and the ergodic spectral
efﬁciency both vanish as N →∞. The key technical ingredient is
a deterministic visibility-annulus block lemma, uniform over all
sufﬁciently large constellations and all "phase states", showing
that a ﬁxed fraction of visible satellites lies in a distance annulus
strictly inside the horizon; this yields explicit ﬁnite-N collapse
bounds. In particular, we derive nonasymptotic O(1/N) upper
bounds on both coverage and ergodic spectral efﬁciency. Finally,
in the case of frequency reuse through independent thinning,
with activity probability q, we show that avoiding densiﬁcation
collapse necessarily requires qN = O(1), equivalently a reuse
factor Ω(N), and we obtain a corresponding explicit O(1/(qN))
upper bound.
Index Terms—LEO satellite constellations, Walker constella-
tion, invariant measure, ergodic dynamical systems, densiﬁcation
converse, interference scaling, SINR coverage, spectral efﬁciency,
frequency reuse.
I. INTRODUCTION
Low-Earth-orbit (LEO) mega-constellations are increasingly
deployed using highly structured Walker designs, where satel-
lites populate a regular two-angle grid and evolve through
coupled orbital and Earth-rotation dynamics [1]. A common
engineering intuition is that densiﬁcation—increasing the total
number of satellites N = NoNs—should improve service
by reducing the typical serving distance and by increas-
ing the likelihood of ﬁnding a strong visible link. Under
full frequency reuse, however, densiﬁcation also increases
the number of simultaneously visible interferers, including
through secondary lobes. This paper establishes densiﬁcation
converses showing that, in Walker constellations under the
invariant (stationary) measure of the dynamics, interference

to collapse as N grows. From a wireless-PHY perspective,
our focus is the downlink performance on a single time–
frequency resource block under full reuse, as in OFDMA-
based satellite air interfaces where many beams/satellites may
reuse the same spectrum. Densiﬁcation reduces the typical
serving distance, but it simultaneously increases the number
of co-channel visible interferers, pushing the system toward
an interference-limited regime unless reuse, scheduling, or
other PHY-layer interference management scales with N. Our
results therefore, provide necessary reuse and activity-scaling
laws for LEO downlinks under standard PHY ingredients: path
loss, antenna gain, fading, and thermal noise. In terrestrial
stochastic-geometry models, densiﬁcation can exhibit regimes
in which the SIR distribution is approximately invariant under
the power-law attenuation assumption. In the present setting,
however, the geometry is fundamentally different: for a ﬁxed
user, the signal power does not increase to inﬁnity with den-
siﬁcation, whereas densiﬁcation necessarily creates a positive-
density population of interferers within the visibility cap. This
forces the aggregate interference to grow with N under full
reuse, and it is precisely this bounded-visibility, rigid-structure
mechanism that drives the collapse converses established here.
What is new (relative to Poisson/BPP satellite models):
The converse mechanism proved here is Walker-structural
rather than purely stochastic-geometric. In Poisson/BPP-type
satellite snapshots on the sphere, densiﬁcation often changes
the geometry in a “smooth” way and one typically studies a
typical conﬁguration. In contrast, Walker constellations form
a rigid two-dimensional lattice on the phase torus, so nearest-
visible association is governed by deterministic regions of the
phase cell over which the serving satellite remains ﬁxed. Our
key Lemma 1 establishes a deterministic, phase-state–uniform
annulus block: once min{No, Ns} is large enough, every phase
state contains a positive-density set of visible satellites at
distances bounded away from the horizon. This uniform block
turns densiﬁcation into an unavoidable, nonasymptotic interfer-
ence lower bound and yields explicit O(1/N) and O(1/(qN))
collapse bounds on SIR with computable constants.
We complement these converses with Monte Carlo simu-
lations in Section VII that explicitly visualize the collapse
mechanism: E[D] decreases with densiﬁcation, yielding initial
gains, but under full reuse, the interference power grows
essentially linearly with N, whereas the signal power saturates,
forcing Pcov and Cerg to collapse beyond a knee. In contrast,
reuse scaling with qN = Θ(1) stabilizes performance.

clustered Cox models, which can be accurate for some
snapshot-level metrics but do not capture the rigid Walker orbit
structure and the associated periodicity/ergodicity needed for a
long-time performance interpretation [1]–[4]. This should also
be contrasted with terrestrial densiﬁcation results: in planar cel-
lular models, the classical singular power-law regime is known
to exhibit SIR scale invariance, while [5] showed that under
physically feasible bounded path-loss models, densiﬁcation
leads instead to ASE saturation or collapse of constrained met-
rics, and that sufﬁciently strong beamforming/antenna scaling
can in principle avoid that terrestrial plateau [5], [6]. Our focus
is fundamentally different. We study the Walker model under
the invariant measure of [1], where nearest-visible association
is constrained by a latitude-dependent visibility cap and the
user–satellite distance has a strictly positive geometric lower
bound. Consequently, unlike in planar singular models, the
useful signal cannot diverge under densiﬁcation even with
pure power-law attenuation, whereas densiﬁcation necessarily
creates a positive-density population of visible interferers. Our
deterministic visibility-annulus lemma makes this mechanism
uniform over the phase state: for every possible value of the
Walker phase variables in the invariant-measure cell, and not
only for an average or typical phase state, a ﬁxed positive
fraction of satellites is guaranteed to lie in a visible distance
annulus strictly inside the horizon. This uniform geometric
property yields the impossibility result that, for sufﬁciently
large N, the ergodic spectral efﬁciency must vanish.
A key technical point is that our bounds are quantitative and
do not rely on heuristics based on the invariant measure. We
prove a uniform (over the invariant-measure state space) deter-
ministic block property: for every phase state in the invariant-
measure cell of the Walker grid and for all sufﬁciently large N,
there exist at least Θ(N) visible interferers conﬁned to a ﬁxed
visibility annulus of distances bounded away from the horizon.
This phase-state–uniform geometric fact converts densiﬁcation
into a hard lower bound on aggregate interference power and
enables explicit nonasymptotic constants.
Concretely, the paper makes the following contributions.
Deﬁne the SINR coverage probability at threshold τ > 0 as
Pcov := P(SINR > τ), and the ergodic spectral efﬁciency as
Cerg := E[log2(1 + SINR)]. All bounds are uniform over the
invariant-measure phase cell (not merely in expectation over
the phase state) and are explicit/nonasymptotic with ﬁnite-N

• Ergodic densiﬁcation converse (general fading). Under
i.i.d. nonnegative fading with unit mean and ﬁnite second
moment, we show that, E[I] grows at least linearly in N,
that Pcov →0 for any ﬁxed τ > 0, and that Cerg →0 as
N →∞. In addition, we obtain explicit O(1/N) upper
bounds (in N = NoNs) for both Pcov and Cerg.
• Nonasymptotic quantitative collapse via a visibility-
annulus block. We establish a deterministic, phase-state–
uniform positive-density annulus block: for all sufﬁciently
large constellations and for every initial phase state in the
invariant-measure cell, at least Θ(N) visible interferers
lie in a ﬁxed visibility annulus bounded away from the
horizon. This geometric mechanism converts densiﬁca-
tion into quantitative (ﬁnite-N) collapse bounds without
relying on a speciﬁc fading law.
• Explicit rate–density rule (general fading). Using only
the unit-mean and ﬁnite-second-moment assumptions on
fading, we derive an explicit constant Kerg < ∞such
that Cerg ≤Kerg/(NoNs) for all sufﬁciently large NoNs,
yielding a necessary density constraint for any target
ergodic rate.
• Necessary reuse/thinning scaling law (general fading).
Under a spatial-reuse model implemented via indepen-
dent thinning with activity probability q, we show that
preventing coverage collapse under densiﬁcation requires
the necessary scaling q NoNs = O(1) (equivalently, a
reuse factor growing at least linearly with NoNs). More-
over, we derive an explicit nonasymptotic upper bound
of order O(1/(q NoNs)).

V. DISCUSSION
The main design implication of Theorems 1–4 is that, in
Walker LEO downlinks, densiﬁcation alone cannot sustain
nontrivial link-level performance under full reuse. The core
reason is the phase-state–uniform annulus-block mechanism
of Lemma 1, which guarantees that, for all sufﬁciently large
constellations and for every phase state, a positive-density
set of visible interferers remains conﬁned to a ﬁxed annulus
away from the horizon. This converts densiﬁcation into explicit
nonasymptotic collapse bounds, rather than only asymptotic or
typical-state statements.
From a system-design viewpoint, the results provide a
direct reuse dimensioning rule. The quantitative bounds in
Theorems 2 and 3 show that both coverage and ergodic spectral
efﬁciency decay at least on the order of 1/N under full reuse,
while Theorem 4 shows that preventing coverage collapse
under thinning requires
qN = O(1),
equivalently
F = 1
q = Ω(N),
with N = NoNs. Thus, increasing the constellation size with-
out commensurate reuse planning, scheduling, beam hopping,
or coordinated muting inevitably drives the system toward
vanishing SINR.
In this sense, the results identify a clear structural limitation
of dense Walker deployments on a shared resource block:
the dominant bottleneck is not the lack of a nearby serving
satellite, but the growth of the co-channel visible interference
population. The numerical results in Section VII illustrate this
mechanism at ﬁnite N and conﬁrm that enforcing the scaling
qN = Θ(1) stabilizes performance, whereas ﬁxed reuse only
delays the collapse.

VIII. CONCLUSION
This paper provided a set of densiﬁcation converses for
structured Walker LEO constellations when the downlink
operates under nearest-visible association and (unless stated
otherwise) full frequency reuse on a common time–frequency
resource block. Our performance interpretation is explicitly
tied to the invariant (stationary) measure on the Walker
phase cell, which is the natural distribution induced by the
constellation dynamics in the rotating Earth frame. Within
this physically meaningful stationary regime, we identiﬁed a
simple but fundamental message: densiﬁcation alone is not a
remedy under full reuse. Increasing the total satellite count
N = NoNs necessarily increases the number of simultane-
ously visible transmitters, and the resulting interference growth
dominates the beneﬁcial reduction in serving distance.

A second design-facing implication concerns reuse planning.
Full reuse is an extreme operating point; a natural alternative
is to activate only a fraction of visible satellites on a given
resource block (via spatial reuse, scheduling, or partitioning
of time–frequency resources). Modeling such reuse through
independent thinning with activity probability q, we derived
a necessary scaling law: preventing coverage collapse under
densiﬁcation requires q N = O(1), equivalently a reuse factor
F = 1/q that grows at least linearly with the constellation size
N. In other words, if the system insists on growing N while
keeping the reuse factor ﬁxed, then collapse is unavoidable;
sustaining nontrivial coverage mandates that the per-resource-
block density of active satellites remain bounded. The asso-
ciated explicit O(1/(qN)) bounds provide a direct rule-of-
thumb for dimensioning the effective reuse factor needed to
maintain a desired coverage level.
Beyond outage and ergodic rate, we also examined whether
densiﬁcation could still be beneﬁcial for the mean SINR ob-
jective JSINR(No, Ns; lu) = E[SINR], an objective sometimes
used as a proxy for average link quality. Using the same
annulus-block argument, we showed that, the mean SINR nec-
essarily decays as O(1/N) for sufﬁciently large constellations
(under a mild small-ball regularity condition on the fading law).
This yields an additional structural consequence: maximizing
JSINR over admissible integer design pairs (No, Ns) reduces
to a ﬁnite search region and therefore admits at least one
optimizer. Thus, even for metrics that might initially improve
with modest densiﬁcation, the Walker-exact model predicts an
eventual decline, and it provides a principled way to localize
the optimizer search.
Taken together, these results sharpen the engineering narra-
tive for dense Walker deployments. When many satellites share
the same time–frequency resource, the dominant bottleneck is
not the availability of a nearby serving satellite but the growth
of co-channel interference from an expanding set of simulta-
neously visible transmitters. Consequently, densiﬁcation must
be accompanied by commensurate interference management—
most basically, scaling reuse (or equivalently limiting the
number of co-channel active satellites)—to avoid operating
in a regime with vanishing SINR, vanishing coverage and
vanishing rate.
The numerical illustration in Section VII supports this
picture at ﬁnite N: serving distances shrink with densiﬁcation,
but under full reuse interference grows nearly linearly in N,
producing a sharp coverage/rate knee and eventual collapse;
enforcing the necessary scaling qN = Θ(1) yields an interfer-
ence plateau and prevents collapse.
Several directions are suggested by the present converses.
First, it would be valuable to complement the necessary reuse
scaling with achievability results under concrete schedulers
(e.g., deterministic reuse patterns across the Walker grid,
coordinated beam scheduling, or graph-based interference
avoidance on the phase torus) and to quantify the constant
factors in realistic parameter regimes. Second, extending the
analysis to multi-beam satellites with beam footprints and
explicit sidelobe models could reﬁne the annulus-block mech-
anism and capture practical antenna-pattern constraints. Third,
incorporating power control, adaptive bandwidth allocation,
and multi-user scheduling at the gateway could clarify which
layers can most effectively compensate for densiﬁcation-driven
interference growth. Finally, extending the framework to multi-
altitude constellations or heterogeneous transmit powers would

Abstract: We establish densiﬁcation converses for Walker LEO constellations under nearest-visible association in the full- frequency-reuse setting. Performance is evaluated under the invariant (stationary) measure induced by the constellation/Earth dynamics on the user–constellation “phase state.” A key Walker- speciﬁc feature, absent from unbounded planar models, is that association is restricted to a bounded visible cap determined by Earth geometry. Under power-law path-loss, a two-level antenna- gain model, i.i.d. nonnegative fading with unit mean and ﬁnite second moment, and nonzero noise, we prove that increasing the total satellite count N = NoNs forces the aggregate interference to grow at least linearly in N, while the useful signal remains uniformly bounded above. Consequently, the downlink SINR cov- erage probability at any ﬁxed threshold and the ergodic spectral efﬁciency both vanish as N →∞. The key technical ingredient is a deterministic visibility-annulus block lemma, uniform over all sufﬁciently large constellations and all "phase states", showing that a ﬁxed fraction of visible satellites lies in a distance annulus strictly inside the horizon; this yields explicit ﬁnite-N collapse bounds. In particular, we derive nonasymptotic O(1/N) upper bounds on both coverage and ergodic spectral efﬁciency. Finally, in the case of frequency reuse through independent thinning, with activity probability q, we show that avoiding densiﬁcation collapse necessarily requires qN = O(1), equivalently a reuse factor Ω(N), and we obtain a corresponding explicit O(1/(qN)) upper bound.
